title: 14 CFR and Publications
summary: Know which source answers the question, what legal weight it carries, and how to confirm that it applies today.
objectives: Locate the rules for pilot privileges, aircraft operation, and accident reporting.
Distinguish regulations, approved aircraft limitations, guidance, and certification standards.
Resolve a practical question with current primary material instead of a memorized acronym or old slide.

sections.title: Start with the question, then choose the rule
sections.body:
A pilot does not need to memorize every paragraph, but must recognize the controlling source and find the applicable text accurately. 14 CFR Part 1 supplies definitions. Part 61 addresses pilot and instructor certificates, ratings, privileges, training, endorsements, experience, and logging. Part 91 contains general aircraft operating rules. NTSB accident and incident reporting is in 49 CFR Part 830, not 14 CFR.

Separate the person from the operation. A pilot can hold the right certificate but lack required recent experience. A current pilot can still be in an aircraft that lacks required equipment or inspections. An aircraft can be airworthy but unsuitable for the weather or planned route.

Apply it: “May I act as PIC?” and “May I log PIC?” are different questions. Find the rule that matches the precise action, pilot qualifications, aircraft, and circumstances.
sections.deep:
Definitions determine scope. When a rule uses terms such as category, class, night, or flight time, look up the applicable definition and any rule-specific qualification before relying on an everyday meaning. A familiar word can have different significance in aircraft certification, airman certification, or a particular operating requirement.

Read the surrounding paragraph, exceptions, and cross-references. A search-result snippet may omit the condition that changes the answer. Explain the reasoning as “This operation has these facts; this paragraph applies because of those facts; these conditions remain to be met.” That produces a more durable answer than memorizing a yes/no conclusion from a different scenario.

sections.title: Regulations and guidance answer different questions
sections.body:
Regulations establish requirements. Approved aircraft operating limitations, markings, and placards must also be followed under § 91.9. The AIM explains flight information and ATC procedures; advisory circulars, handbooks, safety alerts, and similar guidance help explain methods and risks.

Guidance is generally not a separate regulation. An advisory circular can describe an acceptable way to comply without making every sentence an independent legal command. Conversely, calling something “advisory” does not excuse disregarding an actual rule, approved limitation, clearance, or incorporated requirement that applies to the operation.

Apply it: when a training note says “required,” identify the source of that requirement. Is it regulation, an approved aircraft limitation, an instructor endorsement restriction, operator policy, or recommended practice? All can influence your decision, but their authority and scope differ.
sections.deep:
Use guidance to understand the rationale and a sound compliance method, then connect it back to the governing requirement. If a regulation incorporates material by reference, that incorporated requirement can have legal significance that a generic statement about advisory material misses.

FAA Chief Counsel interpretations explain how the agency reads particular provisions and facts. They are important research material, but are not new regulations or a substitute for reading the present rule. An old interpretation can address a superseded rule or different facts. Check date, applicability, later amendments, and whether the interpretation has been superseded rather than treating every letter as a universal binding answer.

sections.title: The aircraft’s approved information controls the aircraft
sections.body:
The AFM/POH and its approved supplements describe the aircraft’s limitations, normal and emergency procedures, performance, systems, and other required information. Use the documents applicable to the actual aircraft, installed equipment, and configuration. Some POHs contain FAA-approved material as well as other manufacturer information; know how the manual identifies each.

A generic model handbook or training slide is useful for learning the layout, but it may not reflect your airplane’s serial number, equipment, modifications, supplements, or current weight-and-balance record. The example empty weight in a lesson is not your airplane’s empty weight.

Apply it: if an avionics installation changes the approved operating capability, consult its applicable flight-manual supplement. A feature visible on the screen does not by itself establish that the aircraft is approved to use it for a particular operation.
sections.deep:
Aircraft-specific information can be distributed across the main manual, supplements, placards, equipment list, and maintenance records. Learn which document answers a question rather than expecting one laminated checklist to contain every condition.

A checklist condenses actions so they can be performed reliably, but the underlying manual explains limitations and contingencies. During training, have the student find the original limitation and explain the condition that activates it. For a real discrepancy or conflict, obtain clarification through the appropriate qualified instructor, maintenance, manufacturer, or FAA channel before relying on an unsupported interpretation.

sections.title: Use each FAA publication for its intended job
sections.body:
SourceBest use
Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical KnowledgeUnderstand aircraft, aerodynamics, navigation, weather, and operational concepts.
Airplane Flying HandbookStudy flight techniques and the reasoning behind maneuvers.
Aviation Instructor’s HandbookDevelop instruction, assessment, communication, and risk-management skills.
Aviation Weather HandbookLearn weather processes, hazards, and information sources.
ACS or applicable PTSIdentify the knowledge, risk management, and skill standards of the practical test.

Advisory circulars provide focused guidance, such as endorsement examples, flight reviews, or airport operations. AC 61-65K is the current endorsement guidance verified for this lesson. Confirm its status before using a particular example.
sections.deep:
The ACS provides an assessment structure, not a complete lesson script and not a substitute for operating regulations. A student should explain an aerodynamic idea, identify its risks, and apply it in an aircraft or scenario; memorizing a list of ACS codes is not the same achievement.

InFOs and SAFOs communicate operational or safety information whose relevance depends on the aircraft and operation. Do not dismiss one solely because it is aimed at operators rather than students. Equally, do not assume every recommended action automatically applies to every trainer. Read the audience, purpose, current status, and references before adding it to a procedure or lesson.

sections.title: Current means the right edition plus the changes since it
sections.body:
Use the effective date and applicability of the particular product. Charts, databases, the AIM, handbooks, advisory circulars, and regulations do not all update on one identical cycle. A current sectional still needs applicable NOTAMs and temporary restrictions; an old saved screenshot is not a current flight briefing.

For a regulatory question, locate the current text and check amendments and effective dates. For an AC, check whether the FAA lists it as active or canceled and whether a newer revision supersedes it. For an aircraft document, verify applicability to the installed configuration and required supplements.

Apply it: keep a small set of authoritative bookmarks: current eCFR text, FAA AIM, FAA advisory-circular search, current ACS, chart products, and the actual aircraft documents. Record the source and paragraph when resolving a question for a student.
sections.deep:
Suppose a slide lists an older endorsement AC revision. The correct response is not to discard all the underlying training; it is to verify the current requirement and current guidance before using the sample. A regulation can remain the same while the recommended endorsement format changes.

When two sources appear to conflict, compare their authority, dates, operation, definitions, and assumptions. A handbook example may be generic while an aircraft limitation is specific. An old article may describe an earlier rule. If the remaining ambiguity affects whether a flight is legal or safe, resolve it before departure rather than choosing the most convenient answer.

sections.title: Accident reporting is a separate post-event duty
sections.body:
49 CFR Part 830 distinguishes accidents, serious incidents requiring immediate notification, preservation of evidence, and written reports. Do not equate every aircraft malfunction with an accident or assume that an incident never needs notification.

Under § 830.5, accidents and specified serious incidents require the operator to notify the NTSB immediately by the most expeditious available means. Examples include flight-control-system failure, an in-flight fire, and an aircraft collision in flight. The list also includes certain other events and an aircraft overdue and believed involved in an accident.

Apply it: first protect life and address the emergency, then promptly determine and meet reporting and preservation duties. A call to the school, insurance company, or FAA does not automatically substitute for the required NTSB notification.
sections.deep:
Definitions matter here too: substantial damage and serious injury have specific meanings in § 830.2. Isolated damage can fall outside “substantial damage” while a separate serious-incident trigger still requires notification. For example, a flight-control malfunction is a notification trigger without needing to prove an accident classification first.

Immediate notification is different from the later written report under § 830.15. The ordinary accident-report deadline is 10 days; an overdue aircraft still missing after 7 days has a separate reporting requirement, and an incident report is submitted when requested by an authorized NTSB representative. Preserve wreckage and records as § 830.10 requires, subject to its life-safety and protective exceptions. Use the current NTSB reporting instructions and complete rule.

teachBack: For a realistic flight, separate pilot qualification, currency, aircraft airworthiness, and operating-rule questions, then identify the source for each.
Show why an ACS standard, an advisory circular, and an approved aircraft limitation have different roles.
Find the current endorsement guidance and verify that the example applies to the intended student operation.
Explain the difference between immediate NTSB notification and a written accident report.
takeaways: Match the exact question to the correct authority and operation.
Read current primary material, including conditions and exceptions.
Approved aircraft limitations and pilot-specific restrictions can be more specific than a generic handbook example.

quiz.question: A pilot asks whether training and an endorsement are needed to exercise a particular pilot privilege. Where should the research usually begin?
options: 49 CFR Part 830
14 CFR Part 61
The airport restaurant’s operating hours
The airplane’s cruise-performance chart
feedback: Part 830 addresses NTSB accident and incident duties rather than ordinary pilot qualification.
Part 61 is the primary starting point for pilot privileges, training, and endorsements.
Airport business hours do not establish airman qualifications.
Performance charts do not establish certificate or endorsement requirements.
quiz.hint: Separate requirements placed on the person from aircraft operating data.

quiz.question: A training note calls an FAA advisory-circular recommendation “a regulation.” What is the best correction?
options: Every AC sentence is independently enforceable as a regulation
An AC can never matter to compliance
Identify the controlling requirement and explain the AC’s guidance role
An AC always overrides an approved aircraft limitation
feedback: Advisory guidance is generally not a separate regulation.
Guidance can explain acceptable compliance methods and can have additional significance when incorporated or otherwise applicable.
The source and authority of the actual requirement need to be established.
An AC does not generally override an aircraft’s approved operating limitation.
quiz.hint: Ask what source creates the duty, then what source explains a method.

quiz.question: A generic POH sample and your aircraft’s current approved supplement give different equipment-operating limitations. What should control the aircraft-specific decision?
options: Whichever value makes the flight possible
The older generic example because it is easier to remember
A social-media summary of the same model
The approved information applicable to the actual aircraft and installation
feedback: Convenience does not establish applicability or authority.
A generic example may not match installed equipment or approved configuration.
A summary does not replace the aircraft’s applicable approved information.
The actual approved aircraft documents and supplements establish the applicable limitation.
quiz.hint: Compare authority and configuration, not just the model name.

quiz.question: What is the role of the flight instructor ACS in a lesson plan?
options: Describe the practical test’s knowledge, risk-management, and skill standards
Replace all Part 61 and Part 91 requirements
Supply the serial-number-specific empty weight of the aircraft
Guarantee that memorizing its codes proves teaching ability
feedback: The ACS organizes the assessment standards that training should prepare a student to meet.
Assessment standards do not replace operating or certification regulations.
The actual aircraft’s current weight-and-balance record supplies that information.
Teaching requires understanding and application, not just code recall.
quiz.hint: Think about what an examiner is evaluating.

quiz.question: The sectional and navigation database are current, but a TFR began this morning. What follows?
options: The TFR cannot apply until the next sectional edition
Current products still require review of applicable temporary notices
The database date automatically incorporates every temporary rule
The flight is allowed if an older screenshot shows no restriction
feedback: Temporary restrictions can become effective between chart editions.
Publication currency and temporary operational changes are separate layers of the information check.
A current database does not guarantee inclusion of every current notice.
An old screenshot cannot establish today’s legal airspace status.
quiz.hint: A valid edition does not mean that no changes have occurred since publication.

quiz.question: A flight-control-system malfunction occurs, but the operator thinks the aircraft has no substantial damage. How should NTSB notification be evaluated?
options: No injury always means notification is unnecessary
Only the insurance company needs a call
The malfunction is a specified immediate-notification trigger under § 830.5
Every incident uses the same 10-day delay before any notification
feedback: Serious-incident notification triggers do not depend solely on injury.
Insurance notification does not replace the NTSB duty.
The listed flight-control-system trigger must be considered even without an accident-level damage conclusion.
Immediate notification and later written-report requirements are distinct.
quiz.hint: Check the listed serious incidents independently of the accident definition.
